message.reasoning:
I'm looking at PeriodFormatterBuilder from Joda-Time and planning JUnit 4 tests that cover its various branches, starting with constructor and clear behavior, assuming joda-time is available on the classpath alongside joda-convert and junit/hamcrest.

I'm mapping out the methods to cover: toFormatter's IllegalStateException when neither printer nor parser exists, toPrinter/toParser returning null when flags are set, the various append methods with their null checks, the numeric field appenders (years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, millis variants), prefix/suffix handling including the composite affix branch when a prefix already exists, and the separator variants with their null validations.

I also need to verify the actual Period printing and parsing logic covering all the print-zero modes, signed value parsing with max digit limits, prefix/suffix scanning through SimpleAffix and PluralAffix, and the composite/separator formatting logic exercised through full formatter round-trips. Since the nested static classes like FieldFormatter, Literal, Separator, and Composite have default package visibility, I can test them directly since my test class lives in the same package.

Now I'm planning out the test methods, using the public API with PeriodFormatterBuilder, PeriodFormatter, Period, PeriodType, and the necessary parser/printer interfaces and MutablePeriod for parsing verification.

I need to check how toFormatter() behaves on an empty builder — tracing the logic around iNotPrinter/iNotParser flags shows that with no elements at all, it should still produce a valid empty-literal formatter rather than throwing.

So to actually trigger the IllegalStateException, I need both flags true simultaneously, but the public append(printer, parser) method already rejects both-null inputs, so there's no direct exposed path to set both flags at once.

I'm sketching out the test cases: one verifying toFormatter() throws when both flags are set, another checking toPrinter() returns null after appending a null printer, and a third checking toParser() returns null after appending a null parser.

Then I'm planning tests for append(null format) and append with both printer/parser null, both expecting IllegalArgumentException, plus tests for appendLiteral covering null input and normal printing output. I'm also outlining appendPrefix tests—null checks, singular/plural null combos, and verifying that calling appendPrefix twice before a field composes affixes correctly via printing—followed by an appendSuffix null-argument test.

Continuing, I'm mapping out appendSuffix tests for singular/plural null, and the IllegalStateException cases when appendSuffix is called with no field yet or after a non-field element like appendLiteral, since literal objects pass the printer/parser equality check but fail the field-formatter instanceof check. I'm also listing individual field tests (years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, millis, and combined seconds/millis variants) along with tests for minimum digit padding, maximum parsed digits, and rejecting signed values.

Now I'm covering the print-zero behavior tests: always printing a field even if its value is zero or unsupported, never printing zero, and the "rarely" variants that force a zero print only on the last or first field when all fields are zero, plus the case where zero prints only if the period type supports that field. Then I move into appendSeparator tests—null argument validation, rejecting adjacent separators, normal separator printing between fields, and separators that only appear if there are fields after them.

I continue into appendSeparatorIfFieldsBefore, the distinction between a regular separator text and a different final-text separator across three fields, full parseInto testing with prefixes and suffixes, malformed input returning a negative position, and confirming clear() resets the builder to a fresh default state. I also want to verify SECONDS_MILLIS and SECONDS_OPTIONAL_MILLIS printing with fractional values, covering both the decimal-places-greater-than-zero and equal-to-zero branches, plus parsing values with explicit '+' and '-' signs.

I'm also thinking about rejected sign values causing a failed parse since '+'/'-' wouldn't register as valid sign characters, leading to no digits found and a negative position returned. I want to cover the parseInt branch for ten-or-more-digit numbers using maximumParsedDigits, as well as the negative-sign branch for shorter numbers. Given time limits, I'll aim for roughly 35-40 test methods with comments flagging uncertain behavior, and I'll need dummy PeriodPrinter/PeriodParser implementations for the append tests, checking whether those interfaces are accessible from this package.

Now I'm recalling the actual Period constructors available in joda-time, settling on using the full multi-arg constructor without a type for standard periods, and the version with an explicit PeriodType for testing restricted types like PeriodType.months() where unsupported fields should trigger exceptions.

I need to check the static factory methods PeriodType offers—millis, seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, years, yearMonthDayTime—to pick the right restricted type for testing PRINT_ZERO_ALWAYS with an unsupported field, wondering whether calling period.get() on a field not covered by its PeriodType would actually throw.

Looking into it, ReadablePeriod's get method likely returns 0 for unsupported fields rather than throwing, which keeps things safe for the test. With that assumption I'm sketching a standard Period with all eight fields set, then a zero-valued Period restricted to a narrower PeriodType to verify the zero-printing behavior.

I'm now drafting the actual test cases: for printZeroRarelyLast and printZeroRarelyFirst, building a formatter with multiple zero-valued fields and confirming exactly one designated field prints "0" while the others are suppressed, tracing through how the formatter's field array determines which position gets the forced zero output.

Now checking printZeroRarelyFirst with the same two fields - I expect Years to print but Months not to, so I need to trace through the logic for the YEARS field type to confirm.

Tracing both cases confirms it: Years outputs with MAX_VALUE not triggered, so "0Y" prints alone, while Months hits the MAX_VALUE return and gets skipped, matching the expected "first field forced" behavior.

I should also test the unsupported-field case where other printers still handle it, then check printZeroNever always returning MAX_VALUE regardless of value. I also want to verify minimumPrintedDigits padding behavior with a three-digit setting.

For maximumParsedDigits, I'm tracing through how the parser limits itself to the first two characters of a longer digit string, leaving the rest unconsumed for subsequent fields to handle.

I should use the high-level parsePeriod method, which requires the entire string to be consumed and throws an exception otherwise, so I need to recall the exact PeriodFormatter API for parsing and parseInto to properly test partial parsing behavior.

These methods do seem consistent with what I remember of the real PeriodFormatter API, so I'll treat them as safe assumptions while noting they're an external dependency not shown in source. I'll keep the tests focused on exercising PeriodFormatterBuilder behavior through this public API.

Now I need to confirm PeriodType factory methods like months(), years(), and standard() for constructing test periods, and plan to check isSupported behavior for combined millis field types.

I'm aiming to keep the test suite reasonably thorough, maybe 40-50 methods, while also examining the appendSeparator internal logic for finding the last separator—particularly a loop that decrements its index twice in certain cases, which looks like a subtle quirk worth testing.

Let me trace through a concrete example with four elements to verify which indices get checked, since the pairing structure means printer/parser objects aren't always identical except for Literal/Separator cases.

Continuing iteration2: --i makes i=1, body checks pairs.get(1), which is the parser slot of pair0. Since printer and parser are typically the same object for Literal/Separator/FieldFormatter entries, checking index1 is equivalent to checking index0 again, so effectively only odd indices matter here for detecting a Separator.

I don't need to trace this low-level loop further - I can verify the behavior through high-level tests instead, like calling appendSeparator twice in a row to confirm it throws an IllegalStateException about adjacent separators.

I want to construct a test with distinct separator text and final text (using the two-argument form), then build a formatter chain with years/months/days and suffixes to verify the correct separator appears when all fields are nonzero.

For the second separator, before is Months (1 field), and after is just Days with count 1, which isn't greater than 1, so it uses the final text "&" — giving "1Y,2M&3D" matching the javadoc exactly. Now I'm considering what happens when months=0 and gets skipped as a regular zero rather than the special last-field case, since years and days are still nonzero.

Since the value isn't zero overall, that field isn't suppressed, so countFieldsToPrint returns 0 for months, meaning the separator logic needs to recurse further into the nested structure—the "after" portion of the outer separator is actually built as its own nested Separator object for the remaining Months/Days pair, and I need to trace how its countFieldsToPrint propagates through the "before" branch with the stopAt threshold.

Since Months has count 0, the inner separator body gets skipped entirely, so Months contributes nothing and the separator text between Months/Days never prints. Days still prints "3D" though, so the whole result collapses to "1Y" + the outer fallback "&" + "3D" = "1Y&3D" -- a nice edge case showing how the final-text fallback kicks in when only one of two later fields actually prints.

Given how intricate this multi-field zero-count branching is, I'm wary of asserting an exact predicted string without being able to run the code myself -- I should flag any such prediction with a comment noting it's derived from manual trace, or better, favor simpler assertions like substring checks or non-exception checks for the trickiest combinations rather than committing to a fully computed expected output.

I'll stick with the unambiguous all-nonzero case I've already confirmed, and avoid the ambiguous zero-skip scenario unless marked uncertain. Now finalizing the test list and moving to write the actual test code with cases I'm confident about, including coverage for seconds-with-milliseconds formatting.

I'm working through negative value handling: with valueLong = seconds*1000+millis negative, integer division truncates toward zero so value stays negative while dp = abs(valueLong)%1000 stays positive, meaning something like -5.250 seconds prints correctly as "-5.250" since the sign carries through the integer part.

I'm also tracing parseInt behavior for negative signs with short vs long digit sequences, handling of a leading '+' skipping a position, and how rejectSignedValues(true) causes a leading '-' to fall into the else branch rather than being treated as a sign, resulting in zero length parsed and no digits found.

I need to verify whether PeriodFormatter.parseInto returns a negative complement position or throws on invalid input, since the convention for failed parses matters for these test cases.

This confirms using parseInto with the negative-value check is legitimate black-box testing against documented API behavior, not reliance on undocumented internals. I'll also use the simpler parsePeriod(String) method for straightforward success/failure cases since it throws IllegalArgumentException on failure.

Now I need to define dummy PeriodPrinter/PeriodParser implementations as static nested test classes, so I'm checking their exact interface method signatures before writing them.

I'll make these interfaces public since they're part of the public API for custom printer/parser combos, and write dummy no-op implementations for testing append(printer, null) scenarios. I should also test the clear() method directly—building a formatter, calling clear(), then verifying toFormatter() produces an empty-pattern formatter that prints "", and confirm the internal field formatter array resets properly.

I want to verify that toFormatter() clones the field formatters array before building, so later appends to the builder don't affect an already-built formatter's shared internal state—this seems like a likely source of the original defect, so I'll test building formatter1, continuing to append fields, then building formatter2, and confirming formatter1's output stays unaffected.

So old FieldFormatter instances keep their reference to the original array, while future appendField calls after toFormatter() modify the cloned array instead - this confirms the clone prevents mutation from corrupting previously built formatters. This is exactly the historical Time-13 bug fix, so I'll write a test demonstrating it.

Then building formatter2 with DAYS added confirms the cloned array is separate from formatter1's original fields. Re-printing with formatter1 afterward should still show the old behavior unaffected, since formatter1 holds references to the pre-clone array -- this is the key regression check: if the clone-before-mutate logic were broken, formatter1 would incorrectly pick up the DAYS field too.

This confirms the formatter should remain "0" even after the builder is reused, directly validating the javadoc guarantee that subsequent builder changes don't affect previously returned formatters. I'll finalize the test code now, importing Period, PeriodType, and MutablePeriod for parseInto verification.

I'm structuring test methods covering minimum-digit boundary cases (0 vs 1 vs 2+ padding branches), appendMillis3Digit's fixed 3-digit field behavior, and sign-handling defaults for parsing signed values like "+5" in appendYears.

I'm also working through the maximumParsedDigits boundary logic when a sign character is present, tracing how the digit limit expands by one to account for the consumed sign and how position/length tracking advances through the loop.

Testing with "+12" and maxDigits=2, after the sign is consumed the limit recalculates to 2, so both remaining digits parse successfully to 12 -- confirming the sign character doesn't count against the max digit limit.

I'll finalize a manageable set of roughly 45 tests, then build a summary table listing each test method alongside the branch or condition it covers, grouping similar ones where reasonable but still listing every method. Now I'm drafting the actual Java test code, adding comments for assumptions like how parseInto handles position and how Period.get behaves for unsupported fields.

I need to double-check the exact method signatures on PeriodFormatter -- print, printTo, parsePeriod, parseMutablePeriod, parseInto, isPrinter, isParser, getPrinter, getParser, withLocale -- based on my knowledge of Joda-Time's API, and proceed with reasonable confidence in these names.

Now I'm sketching minimal dummy printer/parser classes for append tests, throwing UnsupportedOperationException where behavior isn't needed, then planning tests for append(PeriodFormatter) combining a literal inner formatter into an outer one, and append(printer, parser) with custom dummy implementations.

I also need to cover the case where only a printer is supplied with a null parser, checking that toParser() returns null while toPrinter() returns the wrapped printer.

Then I want to combine two append calls on the same builder -- one with a null printer, one with a null parser -- so both flags get set and toFormatter() should throw. I need to trace through carefully how each call affects the iNotPrinter/iNotParser flags since they only flip when the corresponding argument is null, not reset when the other argument is non-null.

I also want to double-check that a default Period with all 8 fields uses PeriodType.standard(), which supports years through millis, matching the field indices used in the formatter tests.

For the unsupported field case, I'm reasoning through PeriodType.months() only supporting months, so combined seconds/millis fields would be unsupported unless PRINT_ZERO_ALWAYS forces the formatter to skip the isSupported check and instead rely on Period.get returning zero for unsupported field types.

Now I'm planning the test file itself, deciding to use the org.joda.time.format package declaration for consistency and to ensure access to PeriodPrinter/PeriodParser if those interfaces turn out to be package-private rather than public.
